summary: A fast-sealing microwave cavity that evacuates samples within 5 minutes of HF etching suppresses niobium oxide regrowth and enables coplanar stripline resonators with intrinsic quality factors exceeding $(2.5 ± 0.3) × 10^6$ at single-photon power. Deliberate re-oxidation after 8 days in air yields a measured Nb$_2$O$_5$ regrowth thickness of $2.5$ nm and a metal–air interface loss tangent of $(2.9 ± 0.7) × 10^{-3}$, providing quantitative control over oxidation kinetics.
motivation: Niobium-based superconducting devices achieve record coherence times but suffer rapid native oxide regrowth after HF etching, which degrades quality factors by suppressing two-level system losses. Understanding and mitigating the metal–air interface loss requires a practical packaging method that preserves chemically treated surfaces on timescales compatible with cryogenic measurement.
method: Four $\lambda/4$ coplanar stripline resonators with gaps from 10 to 100 µm were fabricated on sapphire with 145 nm sputtered Nb, sealed in a copper cavity with indium compression seals and pinch-off tube, evacuated to sub-millibar pressure within 5 minutes post-etch, and measured in reflection at 20 mK; devices were then warmed, exposed to ambient air for 8 days, and remeasured to extract oxide properties from frequency shifts and quality factor degradation.
result: Sealed devices show $Q_{\mathrm{int}} > 10^6$ at single-photon power; after air re-exposure, frequency shifts across all four resonators are consistent with $\Delta t_{\mathrm{MA}} = 2.5$ nm Nb$_2$O$_5$ regrowth (versus 1.8 nm predicted from literature kinetics), and $Q_{\mathrm{int}}$ degradation yields $\tan\delta_{\mathrm{MA}} = (2.9 ± 0.7) × 10^{-3}$, comparable to prior measurements and upper bounds from thermal analysis.
